messages.author: f2069400020b900c
messages.subject: Sampler rejects multinomial logit with random intercepts
parts:
Thanks to all for help with the simple multinomial logit model--it now runs fast and furious. I'm moving toward a multilevel model by estimating one with random (unmodelled) intercepts. At this point the model is rejected because of a problem with indexing b0, the group-level intercepts:

Informational Message: The current Metropolis proposal is about to be rejected because of the following issue:
INDEX OPERATOR [] OUT OF BOUNDS; index=5; lower bound=1; upper bound=4; index position=2; b0

....
 
Informational Message: The current Metropolis proposal is about to be rejected because of the following issue:
INDEX OPERATOR [] OUT OF BOUNDS; index=5; lower bound=1; upper bound=4; inerror occurred during calling the sampler; sampling not done


I can't find the problem in the code, which follows:

data {
  int<lower=2> C;           # num categories of y = 4
  int<lower=0> N;           # num observations = 21855
  int<lower=1> K;           # num variables = 8
  int<lower=1> J;           # num county-years = 62
  int<lower=1> id[N];       # county-years
  int<lower=1,upper=C> y[N];    # categorical outcomes
  vector[K] xmat[N];        # x variables
}
  
parameters {
  matrix[C-1,J] b0_free;      # county-year intercepts
  matrix[C-1,K] beta_free;    # effects coefficients
  vector[C-1] sigma_b0_free;  # intercept variances
  vector[C-1] B0_free;        # level 2 intercepts
}

transformed parameters {
  vector[C] b0[J];
  vector[C] B0;
  matrix[C,K] beta;
  vector[C] sigma_b0;

  for (k in 1:K)
    beta[1,k] <- 0;
  for (c in 2:C)
    for (k in 1:K)
      beta[c,k] <- beta_free[c-1,k];

  for (j in 1:J)
    b0[1,j] <- 0;
  for (c in 2:C) {
    for (j in 1:J) {
      b0[c,j] <- b0_free[c-1,j]; }}

  B0[1] <- 0;
  for (c in 2:C)
    B0[c] <- B0_free[c-1];
  
  sigma_b0[1] <- 0;
  for (c in 2:C)
    sigma_b0[c] <- sigma_b0_free[c-1];
} 

model {
  to_vector(b0_free) ~ normal(B0_free, sigma_b0_free);
  to_vector(beta_free) ~ normal(0,2);
  B0_free ~ normal(0, 10);
  sigma_b0_free ~ cauchy(0, 2.5);

  # likelihood
  for (n in 1:N)
    y[n] ~ categorical(softmax(b0[id[n]] + beta * xmat[n]));
}

I would welcome (again) your advice.

Best,
John

messages.author: 743bbacc59f4b25f
messages.subject: Re: Sampler rejects multinomial logit with random intercepts
parts:
On Thursday, January 22, 2015 at 9:35:05 PM UTC-5, John Sutton wrote:
Thanks to all for help with the simple multinomial logit model--it now runs fast and furious. I'm moving toward a multilevel model by estimating one with random (unmodelled) intercepts. At this point the model is rejected because of a problem with indexing b0, the group-level intercepts:

Informational Message: The current Metropolis proposal is about to be rejected because of the following issue:
INDEX OPERATOR [] OUT OF BOUNDS; index=5; lower bound=1; upper bound=4; index position=2; b0
You tried to stick something into the 5th element of b0 when it is declared to have length 4 for each group here

for (j in 1:J)
    b0[1,j] <- 0;
  for (c in 2:C) {
    for (j in 1:J) {
      b0[c,j] <- b0_free[c-1,j]; }}

I think what happened is that you got the indices backwards. In

vector[C] b0[J];

the first index runs from 1,2, ..., J and the second index runs from 1,2, .., C.

Ben

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: Sampler rejects multinomial logit with random intercepts
parts:
On Thursday, January 22, 2015 at 10:26:18 PM UTC-5, John Sutton wrote:
Jeez you're quick--thanks! I took you to mean that the declaration of b0 should be changed to

vector[J] b0[C];

vector[J] b0[C] is an array with C elements, each of which is a vector of J elements, i.e. you have an array of C J-vectors. So b0[1] is an entire J-vector, as are b0[2], ..., b0[C]. To refer to the jth element of the cth b0 vector you would then use b0[c,j].

though I confess I don't know what that statement really means. Anyway, now it's rejected for a different--but perhaps related--reason, with a series of messages like:

Informational Message: The current Metropolis proposal is about to be rejected because of the following issue:
stan::prob::normal_log(N4stan5agrad3varE): Scale parameter[1]  is -0.407936:0, but must be > 0!

It's telling you that the scale parameter (sigma) of the normal distribution -- which is constrained to be positive  --  has a negative value. 
Is there more to the message that says it's fine if it occurs occasionally? I might be mistaken, but I think if this happens in warmup you should be ok but if it's happening a lot during sampling then something is amiss.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: Sampler rejects multinomial logit with random intercepts
parts:
John,

Everything Jonah has said is correct.

sigma_b0_free needs to be lower bound at zero for efficient sampling. It'll work (sometimes) as you've defined it, but what you want to do is replace:
    vector[C-1] sigma_b0_free; 
with:
   vector<lower=0>[C-1] sigma_b0_free;

That will transform the underlying parameter so you'll always sample a standard deviation component greater than 0.

On Thursday, January 22, 2015 at 10:26:18 PM UTC-5, John Sutton wrote:
Jeez you're quick--thanks! I took you to mean that the declaration of b0 should be changed to

vector[J] b0[C];

vector[J] b0[C] is an array with C elements, each of which is a vector of J elements, i.e. you have an array of C J-vectors. So b0[1] is an entire J-vector, as are b0[2], ..., b0[C]. To refer to the jth element of the cth b0 vector you would then use b0[c,j]. 

 

though I confess I don't know what that statement really means. Anyway, now it's rejected for a different--but perhaps related--reason, with a series of messages like:

Informational Message: The current Metropolis proposal is about to be rejected because of the following issue:
stan::prob::normal_log(N4stan5agrad3varE): Scale parameter[1]  is -0.407936:0, but must be > 0!

It's telling you that the scale parameter (sigma) of the normal distribution -- which is constrained to be positive  --  has a negative value. 
Is there more to the message that says it's fine if it occurs occasionally? I might be mistaken, but I think if this happens in warmup you should be ok but if it's happening a lot during sampling then something is amiss.

--

messages.author: 743bbacc59f4b25f
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: Sampler rejects multinomial logit with random intercepts
parts:
On Thursday, January 22, 2015 at 10:26:18 PM UTC-5, John Sutton wrote:
Jeez you're quick--thanks! I took you to mean that the declaration of b0 should be changed to

vector[J] b0[C];

though I confess I don't know what that statement really means.

This is Stan / C++ is very similar to the R construct of a list of length C where each list element is a numeric vector of length J. So, you could access that in R with

b0[[c]][j]

to obtain the j-th element of the c-th vector. In Stan, it is just

b0[c,j]

or

b0[c][j]
Anyway, now it's rejected for a different--but perhaps related--reason, with a series of messages like:

Declare the standard deviations with a positivity constraint

vector<lower=0>[C-1] sigma_b0_free

Then, you would be two steps closer to having it work.

Ben

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: Sampler rejects multinomial logit with random intercepts
parts:
Now that depends on your intent. To make this
expression compile, you could redeclare
b0 so b0[id[n]] is size C, or you can redeclare
beta to be J x C.

You're using it here:

> for (n in 1:N)
> > y[n] ~ categorical_logit(b0[id[n]] + beta * xmat[n]);

And from looking at that, it doesn't look like you want
either to be a matrix --- that is, beta should be 1 x C,
and b0[id[n]] should be a scalar. After all, y[n] here is
just an integer categorical outcome, so I'd think the right-hand
side would reduce to a scalar.

- Bob

parts:
Okay, thanks very much. I'll have to chew this over a bit.

But just to be clear: this is supposed to be a model with random intercepts (county-level intercepts b0, hyperparameters B0) and effects fixed across counties (beta). b0 is thus C x J (outcome categories x counties), B0 is length C, and beta is K x C (parameters x outcome categories). So beta can't be J x C. I don't know if this changes your diagnosis.

To put a little meat on the bones: These are felony cases, sampled from 12 counties in CA, in which defendants either (1) plead to a felony, (2) go to trial, (3) plead to a misdemeanor, or (4) have their cases dropped. Fun stuff, right?

It might help to see a BUGS model that works (sloooowly):

model{
# level 1 model 
# create multinomial data
for (i in 1:N){
  for (c in 1:C){
    y[i,c] <- equals(adjout[i],c) ;
    }}
# likelihood
for (i in 1:N){
  for (c in 1:C){  
    eta[i,c] <- beta0[id[i],c] + beta[1,c] * cblack[i] + 
    beta[2,c] * clatin[i] + beta[3,c] * sapred[i] + 
    beta[4,c] * detain[i];
  expeta[i,c] <- exp(eta[i,c]) ;
  mu[i,c] <- expeta[i,c]/sum(expeta[i,1:C]) ;
  }
  # distribution of y
  y[i,1:C] ~ dmulti(mu[i,1:C],1)
  }

# level 2 model
for (j in 1:J){

beta0[j,1] <- 0;
    for (c in 2:C){
      eb0[j,c] <- B0[c] ;
      beta0[j,c] ~ dnorm(eb0[j,c], tau_b0[c]) ; }}
  
# priors
B0[1] <- 0 ;
for (c in 2:C){
  B0[c] ~ dnorm(b0_prior[c-1], 1.0E-2) ;
  }

tau_b0[1] <- 0 ; 
for (c in 2:C){
  tau_b0[c] <- pow(sigma_b0[c], -2) ;
  sigma_b0[c] ~ dunif(0, 5) ;

}

for (k in 1:K){

beta[k,1] <- 0.0 ; 
  for (c in 2:C){
    beta[k,c] ~ dnorm(0.0, 1.0E-2) ;
    }}
}  

Thanks again for Stan and for your patient advice.

Best,
John
On Wed, Oct 7, 2015 at 5:05 PM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:

Now that depends on your intent.  To make this
expression compile, you could redeclare
b0 so b0[id[n]] is size C, or you can redeclare
beta to be J x C.

You're using it here:

>    for (n in 1:N)
> >     y[n] ~ categorical_logit(b0[id[n]] + beta * xmat[n]);

And from looking at that, it doesn't look like you want
either to be a matrix --- that is, beta should be 1 x C,
and b0[id[n]] should be a scalar.  After all, y[n] here is
just an integer categorical outcome, so I'd think the right-hand
side would reduce to a scalar.

- Bob
